findings.message: This leaks kernel memory to userspace, and the code reinterprets uninitialized bytes, which is UB. The `_pad` field only covers padding at the `TraceEntry` level. `TraceEvent` is a `#[repr(C)]` enum, so it is a tagged union with uninitialized bytes inside: 3 bytes after `core: u8` in `Dispatch`/`SwitchOut`, 4 bytes between the u32 fields and the u64 in the `Fork*` variants, and the tail of the union for every variant smaller than the largest one (most IPC variants use only 8 of 24 payload bytes). Copying an enum by value (`copy_into` → `*slot = ...`) does not preserve padding, and `trace_event` builds each event on the kernel stack. `from_raw_parts(tmp.as_ptr() as *const u8, ...)` followed by `copy_to_user` can therefore send stale kernel stack bytes to any process. The comment saying 'no uninit bytes' is wrong. Fix: serialize each event field by field into a zeroed byte buffer, or make the ABI a fixed plain-data struct (kind: u32, explicit fields, explicit zeroed padding).

`sys_ktrace` has no privilege check, so any unprivileged user can call it. The data includes kernel stack pointers (`Dispatch.rsp`, `SwitchOut.saved_rsp`) and the user RIP/RSP and PIDs of other users' processes. That exposes kernel addresses and cross-user process activity. The OS enforces multi-user permissions, so this syscall should require euid 0 (or similar), as other privileged operations do.

`dump_trace_rings()` now runs on the ring-3 page-fault path, i.e. every time a user process segfaults. It prints up to 256 entries per core over serial (~80 bytes each). On a 4-core system that is roughly 80KB at 115200 baud, about 7 seconds spent in the exception handler with interrupts disabled on that core. Any unprivileged program can trigger this repeatedly and stall a core, and logs fill with noise for ordinary user crashes. The ring-3 GPF path has the same problem (~line 528). Limit the full dump to kernel-mode faults or panics, or print only the last few entries for user faults.

`core_id as u8` truncates before the bounds check. Values like 256 or 0x100000001 wrap to a valid core and succeed instead of returning an error. Compare `core_id` against `core_count() as u64` before narrowing.

`sys_ktrace` returns at most 64 entries, always the 64 oldest (`copy_into` starts at the chronological beginning), and has no offset or cursor argument. The comment says 'callers can call again for more', but a second call returns the same oldest entries. Userspace can never read the newest 192 entries of a full ring, and those are the most useful ones. Add an offset argument, or copy the newest entries.

Reading another core's ring while that core writes to it is a non-atomic data race through `UnsafeCell`, which is UB under Rust's memory model. It is not just the 'acceptable torn entry' the comment claims. `write_idx` and `count` can also be observed inconsistently, so the start position can be wrong and the whole output misordered. For a live (non-panic) syscall, use a seqlock or atomic indices, or at least document the reordering hazard.

`WakeTask` is only emitted on the immediate-enqueue path. When a wake hits a task that is still `switching_out` (`wake_after_switch = true`), no event is recorded. That deferred wake during switch-out is exactly the race window this phase is meant to diagnose. Record a `WakeTask` (or a separate deferred variant) on that branch too.

The docs contradict the implementation. This section says 'Events appear in chronological order across all cores', and the feature-gate section (~line 173) says `dump_trace_rings()` 'prints the merged timeline'. The code prints each core's ring as a separate block with no merging or sorting. The same doc's earlier section describes it correctly.

The Milestone Goal and the Crash Auto-Dump scope (~line 55) say the dump 'merges all cores into a single sorted timeline', but the implementation prints per-core blocks without merging. Update the docs or implement the merge. Separately, the docs and PR description count 15 instrumentation sites, but the code has 17 (6 scheduler + 4 fork + 7 IPC).
